Living Knowledge Mesh · Organism Study · final build with language

A population of artificial workers with neural-cellular-automaton brains lives on a knowledge graph and learns which facts need attention. This report is generated by python -m lkm.run_all; every number below comes from that run. Python 3.13.16, 4 CPUs, total 176 min. Unit tests: 62 tests, 0 failures, 0 errors.

1. Headline

  • Real data (Overture Maps, NYC, Aug→Sep 2026). Verifying 3% of places, the strongest conventional baseline found a positive on 69.7% of verifications (random: 10.9%). The full organism was -1.8 points vs that baseline [-3.7, -0.4] (LOSS); the cell field alone -1.4 [-3.2, +0.5] (TIE). For one-shot forecasting the cell field changed AUC by +0.0005 [-0.0006, +0.0015] over boosted trees with graph features.
  • Language, system level. Against the previous build's strongest baseline (no text inputs, 64.7% per verification), the final organism finds 68.0%: +3.3 points [+1.9, +5.0] WIN. Most of that comes from reading, which the boosted-tree baseline gets as well once it is given the same inputs; the like-for-like comparison is in the first table.
  • Synthetic worlds. The cell field beat the strongest baseline in: contagion world (+1.5 pts), cascade world (+2.6 pts), lexical world, names unreadable (+1.1 pts). These worlds contain hidden clustered or shifting structure by construction, so this shows when a graph-aware field can help, not that it helps in reality.
  • The 'living' parts. Scent, lifetime plasticity and run-time evolution produced a measurable gain in 1 of 16 paired tests; a measurable loss in 1; the rest were ties.

How to read this: the baseline is a gradient-boosted-tree model with graph features, trained with random label reveals and fine-tuned online, so it receives exactly the information the organism receives. Synthetic worlds are built by me with hidden shared shocks; they show when a graph can help, not that it helps in reality. The real-data row is the one that matters.

First design (v1) and why it was changed

The first version of the workers foraged blind: when they jumped, they jumped to uniformly random patches. On the control world they lost 8 points to a plain ranking, because they could not reproduce a global top-K. The cell field was fine. v2 lets workers sample jump targets from the mesh's own risk field (the genome decides how much to trust it) and trains the NCA and the tree baseline on reveals that look like the game's (the highest-ranked entities are the ones that get verified). v2 was developed on separate development worlds and evaluated on fresh test seeds; the real-data test pools were not used for any design decision. v1 numbers below are on its own test seeds:

2. What was built

  • Cells. A neural cellular automaton on the graph: every node holds a 16-channel state; one shared tiny update rule is applied for 8 asynchronous steps, reading neighbours along space, brand and address edges. It is trained with gradients (JAX) as a residual on top of the baseline, so it starts exactly at the baseline.
  • Workers. A population of individuals with 16-cell recurrent brains (1309 genome numbers). They walk the mesh or jump to random patches, decide where to request a verification, earn energy for confirmed positives and pay for misses. Starving workers are replaced by mutated copies of thriving ones (evolution at run time). Reward-modulated Hebbian fast weights give lifetime plasticity. Discoveries leave scent that diffuses and fades.
  • Evolution. The ancestral genome is evolved with evolution strategies on validation worlds that were never used to fit the baselines, the cells, or the test numbers.
  • Reading. A pretrained sentence encoder (all-MiniLM-L6-v2, ONNX, runs on CPU) reads every place's name and category; website, phone and address strings are parsed into classes; names are compared with their neighbours to spot near-duplicates. All of it comes from the August table only. The boosted-tree baseline receives exactly the same inputs.
  • Speaking. Cells talk to each other in a learned vocabulary of 16 words (communication mode: lex); each cell emits one word per step and, in word-only mode, its neighbours hear nothing else. Workers hear the word the cell field is saying at their node. A narrator turns the organism's state into plain sentences (templates filled with its own numbers).
  • The game. 3% of the entities can be verified over 8 rounds; a verification reveals the true label, and everything revealed can be used afterwards. This models the real constraint: only so many facts can be checked per day.

Mechanism check: does reading names help when the truth is known?

In the lexical world half of each chain's members have no brand link; the chain is only visible through name similarity. With language switched on, every place has a name code and same-name places are joined in the brand relation, for every method alike.

9. Honest limitations

  • The redesign from v1 to v2 was made after seeing v1 results on the control world's test seeds. v2 was developed on separate development worlds and judged on fresh test seeds; the real-data test pools were never used for design, but they are one fixed dataset.
  • With 20 test worlds (synthetic) and 8 spatial test pools (real), intervals are wide enough that differences under about 2 points are not resolvable.
  • Real data has one monthly transition (Aug 19 → Sep 23, 2026). It tests forecasting and sequential verification, not long-term learning or seasonality.
  • The real labels are proxies: 'a name/phone/website/address differs, or the place was removed or closed in Overture'. Overture's own conflation can change records without the world changing. Only 156 of 16188 removals were re-created under a new id and excluded.
  • Overture merges sources, so raw conflicting values are not visible; conflict detection is not tested on real data.
  • Synthetic worlds embody my assumptions about hidden shocks. They are useful to show mechanisms and to falsify (see the control world), not as evidence about reality.
  • Workers see descriptors (risk, scent, age), not text. 'Understanding' in the sense of reading content is out of scope.
  • Language here means a small pretrained sentence encoder plus a learned vocabulary and templated explanations. It is not a large language model; it cannot read web pages or reviews. Words have no fixed meaning across worlds: each model learns its own vocabulary.
  • Some text signals (near-duplicate names next door) probably predict Overture's own merging of records rather than a change in the world. For a knowledge graph with duplicate listings that is also a real signal, but it is a property of this label.
  • The lexical synthetic world is built by me to contain the mechanism it tests.
  • The baseline's and organism's adaptation settings were selected on validation worlds with identical grids; test sets were never used for selection.
